newsitem.title: UK: Russian cobalt spikes, consumers main influence.
newsitem.headline: Russian cobalt spikes, consumers main influence.

text.p: Flurries of consumer buying lifted Russian cobalt in European trading, though one major end-user seemed reluctant to pay higher prices which slowed the pace of the advance, several traders said on Tuesday.
The 99.3 percent grade Russian material moved to around $19.50/$20.50 a pound, up around 50 cents from a week ago.
Traders said consumer demand hit the market in the traditionally slow summer period when stocks run at low levels. Consumer demand is now seen to be the main influence in the metals next direction.
"Usually there is enough material on the ground to satisfy the needs of consumers during the summer period...the market looks to have been caught short," one trader said.
Traders said that a large European chemical company was looking to buy around 50 tonnes of cobalt, but did not disclose the time period over which the purchase would cover.
"At the moment the consumer is helping to cap the market after only buying small amounts, believing that prices are running too high," a trader said.

Other traders said that the recent pricing operation that has pressured prices lower has now bottomed out. "We seem to be in the first stage of a recovery following the recent slide...July/August may see the market around current levels, though I expect prices to rise on demand in September," one said.
Any signs of fresh consumer covering could move prices to $25 a pound given tight market fundamentals, another said.
"Despite the reluctance of some consumers to cover the market is extremely tight," the trader said.

The recent settlement of a strike at Inco's Sudbury, Ontario, operations and news on Tuesday that Russian producer Norilsk's gas supplies returned to normal after being cut by nearly a third during June was noted by traders.
Several said that the loss of production from these areas will be hard to make up in a market suffering from tightness.
Also a trade source with contacts in Russia said that producers in the region were not willing to move large amounts of material after the recent downside pricing operation.
"They seem to be holding off in anticipation of a rise in prices," the trade source said.
